\medskip

\section{Introduction}

\subsection{The problem}
Automated reasoning takes place in a tree. The root is a goal; each node offers finitely many
inference steps; each step spawns a child. If every node offers exactly $b$ alternatives, the
tree has $b^n$ nodes at depth $n$ and exhaustive search is hopeless past modest depths.

What makes search feasible in practice is \emph{pruning}. Most branches can be killed early:
they introduce unsatisfiable side conditions, they loop, they violate a term ordering, they
exceed a resource budget. Once killed, an entire subtree disappears. The surviving structure ---
the partial paths still candidate for extension to a complete proof --- is a sparse, irregular
subtree of the full $b$-ary tree. The question answered here is: \emph{how sparse, exactly?}

\subsection{The answer}
The number is
\[
  \sdim \;=\; \frac{1}{\log b}\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log N(n)}{n},
\]
where $N(n)$ counts surviving prefixes of length $n$. It always exists, it lies in $[0,1]$, and
for finite-state pruning it equals $\log r/\log b$ with $r$ the Perron root of the pruning
automaton's transition matrix.

\subsection{Three strands}
The development braids three classically separate threads.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=2.2em]
\item \textbf{Combinatorics of search trees.} The objects measured are accepted paths in a
pruned tree; the structural input is that a path of length $m+n$ splits into a length-$m$
prefix and a length-$n$ suffix.
\item \textbf{Real analysis.} Existence of the limit is Fekete's subadditive lemma applied to
$a_n=\log N(n)$; the identification of the limit with the infimum gives the theory its
practical bite.
\item \textbf{Spectral theory of nonnegative matrices.} Perron--Frobenius theory supplies, for a
strongly connected automaton, a strictly positive eigenvector that converts the asymptotic
entropy into an explicit eigenvalue.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Contributions}
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2.2em]
\item Definition of a \emph{search profile}, its entropy rate and proof-search dimension, with
proofs that the rate exists, equals the infimum of the finite-scale rates, is nonnegative, and
yields a dimension in $[0,1]$ (\S\ref{sec:profiles}).
\item Submultiplicativity of the path counts of an arbitrary nonnegative
matrix (Theorem~\ref{thm:submul}).
\item The Perron sandwich (Theorem~\ref{thm:sandwich}), proved without any spectral
decomposition.
\item The Bridge Theorem (Theorem~\ref{thm:bridge}) and its dimension form.
\item The Perron Domination Inequality (Theorem~\ref{thm:domination}), namely
$r^n\le\sum_{i,j}(A^n)_{ij}$ for all $n$: an inequality free of any
asymptotics, derived from an asymptotic result.
\item Worked instances: the similarity-dimension case and the Fibonacci automaton with
dimension $\log\golden/\log 2$ and the corollary $\golden^{\,n}\le F_{n+3}$
(\S\ref{sec:instances}).
\end{enumerate}

\section{Setting and motivation for the axioms}

Fix an ambient branching factor $b\ge 2$. A \emph{search space} is a prefix-closed subtree $T$
of the full $b$-ary tree $\{1,\dots,b\}^{*}$. Elements of $T$ of length $n$ are the
\emph{successful prefixes of length $n$}: search states at depth $n$ surviving pruning. Write
$N(n)=\#\{w\in T:\ |w|=n\}$.

Two properties organize everything below.

\smallskip
\noindent\textbf{(P1) Nondegeneracy: $N(n)\ge 1$.} There is at least one live path at every
depth. In a search for a proof that exists this holds by definition; without it the logarithms
are undefined and there is nothing to measure.

\smallskip
\noindent\textbf{(P2) Submultiplicativity: $N(m+n)\le N(m)N(n)$.} A surviving path of length
$m+n$ is determined by its length-$m$ prefix (at most $N(m)$ choices) together with its
length-$n$ continuation. In a shift-invariant search language --- one whose legal continuations
from any live state again form a search language of the same type, which is the case for any
rule depending only on bounded local data --- the number of continuations is at most $N(n)$.
The inequality is typically strict, because most (prefix, suffix) pairs do not concatenate to a
live word.

\smallskip
It bears emphasis how little (P1)--(P2) assume: no self-similarity, no monotonicity, no
regularity, no recursion. The counts may fluctuate wildly. Nevertheless they force a
well-defined asymptotic growth exponent.

One might ask for the raw counts rather than an exponent. But the counts depend on incidental
encoding choices (how many nodes a conceptual step is split into, whether bookkeeping moves are
recorded); the exponent is what survives. Rescaling depth by $\lambda$ multiplies the entropy by
$\lambda$, but if the ambient branching is rescaled compatibly, the ratio $h/\log b$ is
unchanged. The dimension is the encoding-independent content of the counts.

\section{Search profiles, entropy, and dimension}\label{sec:profiles}

\begin{definition}[Search profile]
A \emph{search profile} is a function $N:\N\to\R$ with
(i) $N(n)\ge 1$ for all $n$, and
(ii) $N(m+n)\le N(m)N(n)$ for all $m,n$.
In particular $N(n)>0$, so $\log N(n)$ is defined and nonnegative.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Finite-scale rate]
For $n\ge 1$ put $\mathrm{rate}(n)=\dfrac{\log N(n)}{n}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:ratenn}
$\mathrm{rate}(n)\ge 0$ for all $n\ge 1$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
$\log N(n)\ge\log 1=0$ and $n>0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Entropy rate]
The \emph{entropy rate} of a search profile $N$ is
$h(N)=\inf_{n\ge 1}\mathrm{rate}(n)$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:ratenn} the set of finite-scale rates is
nonempty and bounded below by $0$, so the infimum exists and is finite.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:subadd}
If $N$ is a search profile then $a_n:=\log N(n)$ is subadditive: $a_{m+n}\le a_m+a_n$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
From $N(m+n)\le N(m)N(n)$ with both sides positive, monotonicity of $\log$ gives
$\log N(m+n)\le\log N(m)+\log N(n)$.
\end{proof}

This is the entire bridge between multiplicative combinatorics and additive analysis, and the
reason the axioms were stated multiplicatively.

\begin{theorem}[Search Entropy Theorem]\label{thm:entropy}
Let $N$ be a search profile. Then
\[
  \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log N(n)}{n} \;=\; h(N)\;=\;\inf_{n\ge 1}\frac{\log N(n)}{n}\;\ge\;0,
\]
and $h(N)$ is the greatest lower bound of $\{\mathrm{rate}(n):n\ge1\}$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
By Lemma~\ref{lem:subadd} the sequence $a_n=\log N(n)$ is subadditive, and by
Lemma~\ref{lem:ratenn} the ratios $a_n/n$ are bounded below by $0$; Fekete's subadditive lemma
applies. For completeness: let $L=\inf_{n\ge1}a_n/n$ and let $\varepsilon>0$; choose $m\ge1$
with $a_m/m<L+\varepsilon$. Writing $n=qm+s$ with $0\le s<m$ and iterating subadditivity gives
$a_n\le q\,a_m+a_s$, hence
\[
  \frac{a_n}{n}\;\le\;\frac{qm}{n}\cdot\frac{a_m}{m}+\frac{a_s}{n}.
\]
As $n\to\infty$ with $m$ fixed, $qm/n\to1$ and $a_s/n\to0$ (only finitely many values of $a_s$
occur), so $\limsup_n a_n/n\le a_m/m<L+\varepsilon$. As $\varepsilon$ was arbitrary,
$\limsup_n a_n/n\le L$; the reverse inequality for the $\liminf$ is immediate from the
definition of the infimum. Nonnegativity follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:ratenn}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Why the infimum matters]\label{rem:inf}
The statement $h(N)=\inf_n \mathrm{rate}(n)$ is far stronger than mere existence of the limit:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:inf}
  h(N)\;\le\;\frac{\log N(n)}{n}\qquad\text{for every }n\ge1.
\end{equation}
Any single finite computation of $N(n)$ therefore yields a \emph{proved} upper bound on the
asymptotic entropy, with no error term and no convergence assumption. In most asymptotic
theories a finite measurement is at best evidence; here it is a theorem.
Inequality~\eqref{eq:inf} is also the engine behind Theorem~\ref{thm:domination}.
\end{remark}

\begin{definition}[Proof-search dimension]
For a search profile $N$ and $b>1$, set $\sdim_b(N)=h(N)/\log b$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Dimension bounds]\label{thm:dimbounds}
Let $N$ be a search profile.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\arabic*),leftmargin=2.2em]
\item If $b\ge1$ then $\sdim_b(N)\ge0$.
\item If $b>1$ and $N(n)\le b^n$ for all $n$, then $\sdim_b(N)\le1$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
(1) $h(N)\ge0$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:entropy} and $\log b\ge0$.
(2) The hypothesis at $n=1$ gives $N(1)\le b$, hence $\mathrm{rate}(1)=\log N(1)\le\log b$; by
\eqref{eq:inf}, $h(N)\le\mathrm{rate}(1)\le\log b$, and dividing by $\log b>0$ finishes.
\end{proof}

The proof of (2) is a one-liner precisely because of the infimum characterization: the bound at
scale $1$ already controls the asymptotics.

\begin{remark}[Interpretation]\label{rem:interp}
The formula $h/\log b$ is the \emph{similarity dimension} of classical fractal geometry
transplanted. A self-similar set retaining $s$ of $b$ pieces at each scale has similarity
dimension $\log s/\log b$; a search retaining $s$ of $b$ branches per level has proof-search
dimension $\log s/\log b$. The set of infinite live paths, inside the boundary
$\{1,\dots,b\}^{\N}$ with the ultrametric $d(x,y)=b^{-|x\wedge y|}$ ($x\wedge y$ the longest
common prefix), is a compact, typically Cantor-like set, and the entropy measures its
box-counting size: the ball of radius $b^{-n}$ about a point is exactly the depth-$n$ cylinder,
and $N(n)$ is exactly the number of such balls covering the boundary.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[What the dimension does not see]\label{rem:policy}
The dimension depends only on the counting function, hence on the \emph{geometry} of the search
space; it is invariant under any rearrangement preserving level counts. Two instances may have
identical profiles --- hence identical dimension --- while a fixed traversal policy finds a
proof immediately in one and only after an arbitrarily long detour in the other. Search cost
$=$ geometry $\times$ policy, and the dimension isolates the first factor: exactly the part of
the difficulty no reordering can remove.
\end{remark}

\section{Finite-state pruning and nonnegative matrices}

Let the pruning rule be governed by finitely many states $\{1,\dots,k\}$: the legality of a move
depends only on the current state, and a legal move updates the state deterministically. Encode
this by the \emph{transition matrix} $A\in\R^{k\times k}$ with $A_{ij}$ the number of legal
moves carrying state $i$ to state $j$. Such matrices are entrywise nonnegative; we allow real
nonnegative entries throughout.

\begin{lemma}[Nonnegativity of powers]\label{lem:pownn}
If $A_{ij}\ge0$ for all $i,j$, then $(A^n)_{ij}\ge0$ for all $n\ge0$ and $i,j$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Induction on $n$: $A^0=I$ has entries $0,1$, and
$(A^{n+1})_{ij}=\sum_\ell (A^n)_{i\ell}A_{\ell j}$ is a sum of products of nonnegative reals.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Path count]
For nonnegative $A\in\R^{k\times k}$ set $P(n)=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\sum_{j=1}^{k}(A^n)_{ij}$.
For integer $A$ this is the number of accepted paths of length $n$, over all initial and final
states.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Path counts are submultiplicative]\label{thm:submul}
For every nonnegative $A\in\R^{k\times k}$ and all $m,n\ge0$,
$P(m+n)\le P(m)\,P(n)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For each intermediate state $\ell$ put
\[
  f(\ell)=\sum_i (A^m)_{i\ell},\qquad g(\ell)=\sum_j (A^n)_{\ell j},
\]
the numbers of length-$m$ paths ending at $\ell$ and length-$n$ paths starting at $\ell$. Both
are nonnegative by Lemma~\ref{lem:pownn}, and exchanging summation orders gives
$P(m)=\sum_\ell f(\ell)$ and $P(n)=\sum_\ell g(\ell)$. Expanding $A^{m+n}=A^mA^n$ entrywise and
reordering the finite triple sum,
\[
  P(m+n)=\sum_i\sum_j\sum_\ell (A^m)_{i\ell}(A^n)_{\ell j}
        =\sum_\ell\Big(\sum_i (A^m)_{i\ell}\Big)\Big(\sum_j (A^n)_{\ell j}\Big)
        =\sum_\ell f(\ell)g(\ell).
\]
Meanwhile $P(m)P(n)=\sum_\ell f(\ell)\big(\sum_{\ell'}g(\ell')\big)$. Since all
$g(\ell')\ge0$ we have $g(\ell)\le\sum_{\ell'}g(\ell')$; multiplying by $f(\ell)\ge0$ and
summing over $\ell$ gives the claim.
\end{proof}

Conceptually: concatenation requires the endpoint of the first path to match the start of the
second, whereas $P(m)P(n)$ pays for \emph{all} pairings; the defect is the mismatched pairs.

\begin{corollary}[Automaton profile]\label{cor:autprofile}
If in addition $P(n)\ge1$ for all $n$, then $P$ is a search profile and Theorems
\ref{thm:entropy} and \ref{thm:dimbounds} apply to it.
\end{corollary}

\begin{lemma}[Eigenvectors of powers]\label{lem:eigpow}
If $Av=rv$ then $A^n v=r^n v$ for all $n\ge0$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Induction: $A^0v=v$, and $A^{n+1}v=A(r^nv)=r^n(Av)=r^{n+1}v$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Perron sandwich]\label{thm:sandwich}
Let $A\in\R^{k\times k}$ be nonnegative and suppose there exist $v\in\R^k$, constants
$0<c\le C$, and $r\in\R$ with $c\le v_i\le C$ for all $i$ and $Av=rv$. Then for every $n\ge0$,
\[
  c\,P(n)\;\le\;r^n\sum_i v_i\;\le\;C\,P(n).
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
By Lemma~\ref{lem:eigpow}, for each row $i$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:row}
  \sum_j (A^n)_{ij}\,v_j \;=\; r^n v_i,
\end{equation}
and all $(A^n)_{ij}\ge0$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:pownn}. Replacing $v_j$ by $c\le v_j$ in
\eqref{eq:row} decreases the left side termwise, giving
$c\sum_j (A^n)_{ij}\le r^n v_i$; summing over $i$ yields the left inequality. Replacing $v_j$ by
$C\ge v_j$ increases it termwise, giving $r^nv_i\le C\sum_j (A^n)_{ij}$; summing over $i$ yields
the right one.
\end{proof}

The proof uses no spectral decomposition, no Jordan form, no complex analysis, and no assumption
that $r$ is the largest eigenvalue. All that is needed is one eigenvector with coordinates
bounded away from $0$ and $\infty$. For irreducible $A$ (equivalently, strongly connected
automaton) such a $v$ exists by Perron--Frobenius with $r=\rho(A)$; the theorem isolates exactly
the consequence the analysis requires.

\begin{remark}\label{rem:theta}
Writing $S=\sum_i v_i$, the sandwich reads
$\frac{S}{C}r^n\le P(n)\le\frac{S}{c}r^n$: path counts are exponential with base exactly $r$,
up to a bounded multiplicative fluctuation in $[S/C,S/c]$ whose width $C/c$ is the spread of
the eigenvector.
\end{remark}

\section{The Bridge Theorem}

\begin{lemma}[Logarithmic squeeze]\label{lem:squeeze}
Let $N:\N\to\R$ and suppose there are $0<c'\le C'$ and $r>0$ with $c'r^n\le N(n)\le C'r^n$ for
all $n$. Then $\lim_{n\to\infty}\log N(n)/n=\log r$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For any $\kappa>0$, $\log(\kappa r^n)/n=\log\kappa/n+\log r\to\log r$. Applying this to
$\kappa=c'$ and $\kappa=C'$ and using monotonicity of $\log$ on the sandwich (all quantities
positive) squeezes $\log N(n)/n$ between two sequences with limit $\log r$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Bridge Theorem]\label{thm:bridge}
Let $k\ge1$, let $A\in\R^{k\times k}$ be nonnegative, and suppose $A$ admits an eigenvector $v$
with $0<c\le v_i\le C$ for an eigenvalue $r>0$. Then
\[
  \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log P(n)}{n}\;=\;\log r,\qquad P(n)=\sum_{i,j}(A^n)_{ij}.
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Put $S=\sum_i v_i$. Since $k\ge1$ and $v_i\ge c>0$, $S>0$; also $C\ge c>0$. By
Theorem~\ref{thm:sandwich}, $\tfrac{S}{C}r^n\le P(n)\le\tfrac{S}{c}r^n$ for all $n$, with
$0<S/C\le S/c$. Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:squeeze}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Dimension form]\label{cor:dimform}
Under the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:bridge} and for $b>1$,
\[
  \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log P(n)}{n\log b}\;=\;\frac{\log r}{\log b}.
\]
The proof-search dimension of a Perron-controlled finite-state pruned search inside a $b$-ary
tree is $\log r/\log b$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[Fekete meets Perron]\label{thm:fekperron}
Let $A$ be as in Theorem~\ref{thm:bridge} and assume $P(n)\ge1$ for all $n$, so $P$ is a search
profile. Then $h(P)=\inf_{n\ge1}\log P(n)/n=\log r$, and $\sdim_b(P)=\log r/\log b$ for $b>1$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Theorem~\ref{thm:entropy} gives $\log P(n)/n\to h(P)$ and Theorem~\ref{thm:bridge} gives
$\log P(n)/n\to\log r$; limits in $\R$ are unique. Divide by $\log b$ for the second claim.
\end{proof}

This is the sharpest form of the bridge: the Fekete infimum, a purely analytic object defined by
an infimum over all scales, coincides with the logarithm of a Perron eigenvalue.

\begin{theorem}[Perron Domination Inequality]\label{thm:domination}
Let $A\in\R^{k\times k}$ ($k\ge1$) be nonnegative with $P(n)\ge1$ for all $n$, and suppose $A$
admits an eigenvector $v$ with $0<c\le v_i\le C$ for an eigenvalue $r>0$. Then for
\emph{every} $n\ge0$,
\[
  r^n\;\le\;\sum_{i,j}(A^n)_{ij}.
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For $n=0$ the claim is $1\le P(0)$, which is a hypothesis. For $n\ge1$, Theorem
\ref{thm:fekperron} gives $h(P)=\log r$, and \eqref{eq:inf} applied to the profile $P$ gives
$\log r\le\log P(n)/n$. Multiplying by $n>0$ gives $\log(r^n)\le\log P(n)$; both arguments are
positive, so strict monotonicity of $\log$ on $(0,\infty)$ yields $r^n\le P(n)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
Theorem~\ref{thm:domination} contains no limits, no asymptotics, and no error terms: it is a
finite inequality about matrix powers valid at every $n$. Yet the proof runs through an entropy
that only exists in the limit. This is the leverage provided by the infimum half of Fekete's
lemma: an asymptotic quantity that is simultaneously a uniform lower bound on all finite-scale
rates transfers information from $n=\infty$ back to every finite $n$.
\end{remark}

\section{Worked instances}\label{sec:instances}

\subsection{The scalar case: recovering the similarity dimension}

Take $k=1$ and $A=(s)$ with $s>0$: a uniformly self-similar search in which exactly $s$ of the
available branches extend to a proof, with no state dependence.

\begin{proposition}
$P(n)=s^n$ for all $n\ge0$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
$A^n=(s^n)$ by induction, and the sum of entries of a $1\times1$ matrix is its unique entry.
\end{proof}

The vector $v=(1)$ is a positive eigenvector with $r=s$ and $c=C=1$, so
Theorem~\ref{thm:bridge} applies.

\begin{theorem}[Similarity dimension]
For $s>0$ and $b>1$,
$\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log P(n)}{n\log b}=\frac{\log s}{\log b}$.
\end{theorem}

Sanity checks: $s=b$ gives dimension $1$ (no pruning); $s=1$ gives dimension $0$ (a single live
path, search is deterministic); $s=2,b=3$ gives $\log2/\log3\approx0.6309$, the dimension of the
middle-thirds Cantor set --- and indeed the boundary of the surviving tree \emph{is} a Cantor
set in that case. The general theory therefore strictly extends fractal similarity dimension,
replacing exact self-similarity by mere submultiplicativity.

\subsection{The Fibonacci pruning automaton and the golden ratio}

Inside the binary search tree ($b=2$), impose the rule: \emph{never use two ``expensive''
inference steps in a row}. At each node one available move is expensive (a case split, a heavy
decision procedure, an instantiation of a costly lemma) and the other is cheap. One bit of
memory suffices: state $1$ = ``last move cheap'', state $2$ = ``last move expensive''. From
state $1$ both moves are legal; from state $2$ only the cheap one, returning to state $1$. The
transition matrix is
\[
  A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}.
\]

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:fibsq}
$A^2=A+I$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
$A^2=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}
    =\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}+\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Fibonacci recursion]\label{prop:fibrec}
$P(n+2)=P(n+1)+P(n)$ for all $n\ge0$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
By Lemma~\ref{lem:fibsq}, $A^{n+2}=A^n(A+I)=A^{n+1}+A^n$; summing all entries (a linear
operation) gives the recursion.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Path counts are Fibonacci numbers]\label{thm:fibcount}
With $F_1=F_2=1$ and $F_{m+2}=F_{m+1}+F_m$, we have $P(n)=F_{n+3}$ for all $n\ge0$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Base cases: $P(0)=\sum_{i,j}I_{ij}=2=F_3$ and $P(1)=1+1+1+0=3=F_4$. The inductive step is
Proposition~\ref{prop:fibrec} together with $F_{n+5}=F_{n+4}+F_{n+3}$.
\end{proof}

So the surviving prefix counts are $2,3,5,8,13,21,34,55,89,\dots$

\begin{lemma}[Golden eigenvector]\label{lem:goldvec}
Let $\golden=(1+\sqrt5)/2$, the positive root of $\lambda^2=\lambda+1$. Then
\[
  A\begin{pmatrix}\golden\\1\end{pmatrix}
  =\begin{pmatrix}\golden+1\\ \golden\end{pmatrix}
  =\golden\begin{pmatrix}\golden\\1\end{pmatrix},
\]
using $\golden^2=\golden+1$. Its coordinates satisfy $1\le v_i\le\golden$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Golden-ratio proof-search dimension]\label{thm:golddim}
The Fibonacci-pruned binary search space has proof-search dimension
\[
  \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log P(n)}{n\log 2}\;=\;\frac{\log\golden}{\log 2}\;\approx\;0.694242.
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Apply Corollary~\ref{cor:dimform} with $k=2$, $A$ as above (nonnegative), $v=(\golden,1)$,
$c=1$, $C=\golden$, $r=\golden>0$, $b=2>1$.
\end{proof}

\noindent\textbf{Interpretation.} A single bit of memory in the pruning rule reduces the
dimension from $1$ to $\approx0.6942$. At depth $100$ the unpruned binary tree has
$2^{100}\approx1.27\times10^{30}$ nodes while the pruned tree has
$F_{103}\approx1.5\times10^{21}$ --- a reduction by more than eight orders of magnitude, with
the gap growing as $2^{0.3058\,n}$. Pruning does not turn an exponential problem polynomial; it
lowers the base of the exponential, and the dimension records precisely by how much.

\begin{corollary}[Golden powers dominated by Fibonacci numbers]\label{cor:goldfib}
For every $n\ge0$, $\golden^{\,n}\le F_{n+3}$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
All hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:domination} hold: $A$ is nonnegative, $P(n)=F_{n+3}\ge1$, and
$(\golden,1)$ is a positive eigenvector for $r=\golden>0$. Hence
$\golden^{\,n}\le P(n)=F_{n+3}$.
\end{proof}

Numerically $\golden^{10}\approx122.99\le233=F_{13}$ and
$\golden^{20}\approx15127.0\le28657=F_{23}$. The ratio $F_{n+3}/\golden^{\,n}$ tends to
$\golden^3/\sqrt5\approx1.894$, consistent with the sandwich constants
$S/C=(\golden+1)/\golden\approx1.618$ and $S/c=\golden+1\approx2.618$ of
Remark~\ref{rem:theta}.

\section{Algorithms}

\subsection{Certified entropy bracketing}
Given a procedure computing $N(n)$ and a depth budget $M$, output
$\overline h=\min_{1\le n\le M}\log N(n)/n$. By \eqref{eq:inf} this is an unconditional upper
bound on the entropy, whatever the profile does beyond depth $M$. In the Perron-controlled case,
Remark~\ref{rem:theta} also gives $\log P(n)/n\ge\log r+\log(S/C)/n$, so the finite-scale rate
overestimates $\log r$ by at most $|\log(C/c)|/n$: the bracket has width $O(1/n)$ and is
explicitly certifiable. For a $k\times k$ automaton, computing $P(1),\dots,P(M)$ costs
$O(Mk^3)$ arithmetic operations by iterated matrix multiplication, or $O(Mk^2)$ by propagating
the row-sum vector $u^{(n)}=A^n\mathbf 1$, since $P(n)=\mathbf 1^{\top}u^{(n)}$ and
$u^{(n+1)}=Au^{(n)}$.

\subsection{Perron root by scaled power iteration}
Iterate $x^{(n+1)}=Ax^{(n)}/\|Ax^{(n)}\|_1$ from a positive start and estimate $r$ by
$\|Ax^{(n)}\|_1$. Under primitivity convergence is geometric with ratio $|\lambda_2|/r$; each
iteration costs $O(k^2)$. The output is self-certifying: with $\underline r=\min_i(Av)_i/v_i$
and $\overline r=\max_i(Av)_i/v_i$, the Collatz--Wielandt inequalities give
$\underline r\le r\le\overline r$, and Theorem~\ref{thm:sandwich} applied with $\underline r$
and $\overline r$ yields rigorous two-sided bounds on $P(n)$ for all $n$.

\subsection{Automaton synthesis from a local pruning rule}
Given a pruning predicate depending on the last $w$ moves in a $b$-ary tree, take the states to
be the legal windows of length $w-1$ and set $A_{uv}=1$ when $v$ arises from $u$ by appending a
legal symbol and dropping the first. The matrix has at most $b^{\,w-1}$ rows and at most $b$
nonzeros per row. This is the standard construction of a sofic subshift from finitely many
forbidden words; the resulting dimension $\log\rho(A)/\log b$ is its normalized topological
entropy. The Fibonacci automaton is the case $b=2$, $w=2$, forbidden word
``expensive-expensive''.

\section{Discussion}

\subsection{What has been achieved}
Three points deserve emphasis. First, the \emph{generality} of the existence theorem: nothing
beyond $N(n)\ge1$ and submultiplicativity is assumed --- no self-similarity, no uniform
branching, no memorylessness, no monotonicity. Second, \emph{finite computations are theorems}:
the identification of the limit with the infimum turns any finite prefix count into a proved
upper bound, and combined with the Perron lower bound makes the dimension explicitly
bracketable. Third, the bridge is \emph{two-way}: the reverse consequence
$r^n\le\sum_{i,j}(A^n)_{ij}$, specializing to $\golden^{\,n}\le F_{n+3}$, shows information
flowing from asymptotic entropy back to uniform finite inequalities in linear algebra.

\subsection{Relation to neighbouring theories}
For a finite-state pruning rule the set of infinite accepted paths is a \emph{sofic shift} and
the entropy is its topological entropy $\log\rho(A)$; the novelty is the proof-search reading
--- the ambient normalization by $\log b$, the interpretation of $\sdim$ as a density of
surviving proof attempts, and the extension of the existence statement to arbitrary
submultiplicative profiles that need not come from any shift. The dimension is the similarity
dimension of fractal geometry (Remark~\ref{rem:interp}), and the scalar case shows the
generalization is conservative. A Galton--Watson tree with mean offspring $\mu$ has, almost
surely on survival, boundary Hausdorff dimension $\log\mu/\log b$; the present theory is the
deterministic analogue with the Perron root playing the role of $\mu$. Finally, in proof
complexity the dimension is a lower-bound-friendly quantity, bounding below the abundance of
nodes any complete search must be prepared to examine, uniformly in the traversal policy.

\subsection{Limitations}
(i) Theorem~\ref{thm:bridge} assumes a positive eigenvector; for irreducible $A$ this follows
from Perron--Frobenius, but reducible matrices --- where the spectral radius may be realized
only on a subset of states --- are not covered. (ii) Dimension is not cost
(Remark~\ref{rem:policy}). (iii) The box-counting/entropy identity is established; identifying
it with Hausdorff dimension requires a mass-distribution argument.

\section{Future directions}

\begin{conjecture}[Hausdorff dimension of the boundary]
Let $N(n)$ count successful prefixes of length $n$ in a finitely branching search language with
$N(n+m)\le N(n)N(m)$ and $N(n)\ge1$. The normalized logarithmic growth rate exists and equals
the infimum of the finite-scale rates (proved above). Under a compatible ultrametric and a
finite-type extension condition, this rate also equals the Hausdorff dimension of the infinite
successful-path boundary.
\end{conjecture}
\noindent The insight is that exact additivity of finite profiles is replaced by subadditivity
while the relative-entropy normalization survives intact; a mass-distribution principle applied
to the measure defined by the Perron eigenvector on cylinders is the natural route.

\begin{conjecture}[Ergodic branching]
For a stationary ergodic sequence of ambient and successful branching pairs $(B_n,S_n)$ with
$1\le S_n\le B_n$ and suitable logarithmic integrability, the almost-sure proof-search dimension
is $\Ex[\log S_0]/\Ex[\log B_0]$.
\end{conjecture}
\noindent Logarithmic path volumes are additive cocycles, so their ratio should converge by
ergodic averaging; the deterministic theory supplies the exact finite-block identity whose
random-block limit this predicts.

\begin{conjecture}[Dimension spectrum and realizability]
For successful paths accepted by a strongly connected finite-state pruning automaton over a
fixed $b$-ary tree, the dimension equals $\log\rho(A)/\log b$ with $\rho(A)$ the spectral radius
of the automaton's nonnegative transition matrix. Moreover every algebraic number arising as
such a normalized Perron root is realizable by a finite-state proof-search geometry.
\end{conjecture}
\noindent Corollary~\ref{cor:dimform} proves the dimension formula under the explicit hypothesis
of a positive eigenvector; removing it in favour of irreducibility needs the full
Perron--Frobenius existence theorem. A route covering even reducible matrices is Gelfand's
formula $\rho(A)=\lim_n\|A^n\|^{1/n}$, since $P(n)$ is the sum-of-entries norm of $A^n$ and that
norm is submultiplicative by Theorem~\ref{thm:submul}. Scalar products of branching numbers
generalize to matrix products, with Perron growth replacing ordinary multiplication.

\begin{conjecture}[Policy-sensitive cost at fixed dimension]
For every rational $d\in(0,1)$ and every computable unbounded $f$, there are two finitely
branching search instances with the same successful-prefix dimension $d$ but deterministic
depth-first discovery costs whose ratio exceeds $f(n)$ at infinitely many depths.
\end{conjecture}
\noindent Dimension measures abundance whereas a policy measures ordering; adversarial
rearrangement preserves all prefix counts while moving successful terminals arbitrarily late.

\begin{conjecture}[Stability under sparse perturbations]
If two nonstationary branching profiles differ on a set of levels of asymptotic density zero and
their branching numbers are uniformly bounded above and bounded below away from unary
degeneration, their limiting relative-entropy dimensions agree whenever either limit exists.
\end{conjecture}
\noindent Sparse changes contribute only sublinear error to both logarithmic volumes; repetition
invariance and weighted composition supply the finite-block algebra needed to quantify the
effect of exceptional blocks.

\section{Conclusion}

A proof-search space possesses a dimension. It exists under hypotheses so weak --- nondegeneracy
and submultiplicativity of prefix counts --- that essentially any realistic search satisfies
them. It is normalized to $[0,1]$, with $0$ meaning ``essentially a single path'' and $1$ meaning
``pruning has failed''. Every finite measurement of prefix counts is a rigorous upper bound on
it. And whenever the pruning rule is implementable with finite memory, the dimension is not an
abstraction but an eigenvalue: take the transition matrix, compute its Perron root $r$, read off
$\log r/\log b$.

The theory is conservative --- it recovers classical similarity dimension in the uniform case ---
and it produces recognizable constants in the simplest nontrivial instance: forbidding two
consecutive expensive inference steps in a binary search tree yields Fibonacci prefix counts,
golden-ratio growth, and dimension $\log\golden/\log2\approx0.6942$. Running the bridge backwards
recovers $\golden^{\,n}\le F_{n+3}$, a finite inequality obtained from an asymptotic theorem
because Fekete's limit is an infimum.

Beyond the specific theorems, the framework offers a way of thinking. Exponential growth is
exponential growth, whether it occurs in a fractal, in the powers of a nonnegative matrix, or in
the branching tree of everything one might try next. Once the three settings are recognized as
the same setting, results transfer freely in every direction.

"""
Submultiplicative Search Entropy and the Perron Root
====================================================

Numerical demonstrations of the proof-search dimension theory.

The theory in one paragraph
---------------------------
Let N(n) count the "successful prefixes" of length n in a pruned search tree:
partial search paths of depth n that have not yet been killed.  Two hypotheses
suffice for everything:

    (P1)  N(n) >= 1                       (nondegeneracy)
    (P2)  N(m + n) <= N(m) * N(n)         (submultiplicativity)

Then the finite-scale rates log N(n) / n converge, and the limit -- the
ENTROPY RATE h -- equals the INFIMUM of those rates.  Normalizing by the
ambient branching factor b gives the PROOF-SEARCH DIMENSION

    dim = h / log b   in   [0, 1].

For finite-state pruning with nonnegative transition matrix A, the path counts
P(n) = sum of all entries of A^n are submultiplicative, and if A has an
eigenvector v with 0 < c <= v_i <= C for eigenvalue r > 0 then

    c * P(n)  <=  r^n * sum(v)  <=  C * P(n)          (Perron sandwich)

so h = log r and dim = log r / log b (the Bridge Theorem).  Running the
infimum characterization backwards gives, for every n,

    r^n <= sum_{i,j} (A^n)_{ij}                       (Perron domination)

which for the "no two consecutive expensive steps" automaton in the binary
tree specializes to  phi^n <= F(n+3),  with dim = log phi / log 2 ~ 0.6942.

This file is self-contained: standard library only, all helpers inlined.
Run with:   python3 demo.py
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from typing import Callable, Iterable, List, Sequence, Tuple

Matrix = List[List[float]]
Vector = List[float]

SEP = "=" * 78
SUB = "-" * 78


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Basic linear algebra (pure Python, no dependencies)
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def mat_mul(A: Matrix, B: Matrix) -> Matrix:
    """Ordinary matrix product.  Cost O(k^3) for k x k inputs."""
    n, m, p = len(A), len(B), len(B[0])
    return [[sum(A[i][t] * B[t][j] for t in range(m)) for j in range(p)]
            for i in range(n)]


def mat_vec(A: Matrix, v: Vector) -> Vector:
    """Matrix-vector product A v.  Cost O(k^2)."""
    return [sum(A[i][j] * v[j] for j in range(len(v))) for i in range(len(A))]


def identity(k: int) -> Matrix:
    return [[1.0 if i == j else 0.0 for j in range(k)] for i in range(k)]


def mat_pow(A: Matrix, n: int) -> Matrix:
    """A^n by binary exponentiation.  Cost O(k^3 log n)."""
    result = identity(len(A))
    base = [row[:] for row in A]
    while n > 0:
        if n & 1:
            result = mat_mul(result, base)
        base = mat_mul(base, base)
        n >>= 1
    return result


def path_count(A: Matrix, n: int) -> float:
    """P(n) = sum of ALL entries of A^n: the number of accepted length-n paths."""
    return sum(sum(row) for row in mat_pow(A, n))


def path_counts_upto(A: Matrix, m: int) -> List[float]:
    """P(0), ..., P(m) in O(m k^2) by propagating the row-sum vector u = A^n 1."""
    k = len(A)
    u: Vector = [1.0] * k          # u = A^0 * 1
    out: List[float] = []
    for _ in range(m + 1):
        out.append(sum(u))
        u = mat_vec(A, u)
    return out


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The two headline constants
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

PHI: float = (1.0 + math.sqrt(5.0)) / 2.0          # golden ratio ~ 1.6180339887
FIB_MATRIX: Matrix = [[1.0, 1.0],
                      [1.0, 0.0]]                   # "no two expensive steps in a row"


def fibonacci(m: int) -> int:
    """F(1) = F(2) = 1, F(m+2) = F(m+1) + F(m); F(0) = 0."""
    a, b = 0, 1
    for _ in range(m):
        a, b = b, a + b
    return a


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Search profiles: entropy rate and proof-search dimension
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def finite_scale_rate(N: Callable[[int], float], n: int) -> float:
    """rate(n) = log N(n) / n, the average branching entropy out to depth n."""
    if n < 1:
        raise ValueError("finite-scale rates are defined for n >= 1")
    return math.log(N(n)) / n


def entropy_upper_bound(N: Callable[[int], float], depth: int) -> float:
    """
    CERTIFIED upper bound on the entropy rate: min over 1 <= n <= depth of
    log N(n) / n.  Because the Fekete limit is the INFIMUM of the finite-scale
    rates, this is not an estimate -- it is a proved bound on h, valid no
    matter how the profile behaves beyond `depth`.
    """
    return min(finite_scale_rate(N, n) for n in range(1, depth + 1))


def proof_search_dimension(entropy: float, b: float) -> float:
    """dim = h / log b, the ambient-normalized (fractal) dimension."""
    return entropy / math.log(b)


def check_submultiplicative(N: Callable[[int], float], bound: int) -> Tuple[bool, float]:
    """
    Verify N(m+n) <= N(m) N(n) for all 0 <= m, n <= bound and report the worst
    "defect ratio" N(m+n) / (N(m) N(n)) observed.  A ratio of 1 means the
    inequality is tight; smaller ratios measure how many (prefix, suffix)
    pairs fail to concatenate into a live path.
    """
    ok = True
    worst = 0.0
    for m in range(bound + 1):
        for n in range(bound + 1):
            lhs, rhs = N(m + n), N(m) * N(n)
            if lhs > rhs * (1 + 1e-12):
                ok = False
            worst = max(worst, lhs / rhs)
    return ok, worst


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Perron machinery
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def perron_root_power_iteration(
    A: Matrix, iters: int = 400, tol: float = 1e-15
) -> Tuple[float, Vector]:
    """
    Scaled power iteration x <- A x / ||A x||_1 from a positive start.
    Returns (r, v) with v normalized so that min(v) = 1.
    Cost O(k^2) per iteration; geometric convergence at rate |lambda_2| / r.
    """
    k = len(A)
    x: Vector = [1.0 / k] * k
    r = 0.0
    for _ in range(iters):
        y = mat_vec(A, x)
        norm = sum(abs(t) for t in y)
        if norm == 0.0:
            return 0.0, x
        new_x = [t / norm for t in y]
        if max(abs(new_x[i] - x[i]) for i in range(k)) < tol:
            x, r = new_x, norm
            break
        x, r = new_x, norm
    lo = min(x)
    v = [t / lo for t in x] if lo > 0 else x
    return r, v


def collatz_wielandt_bracket(A: Matrix, v: Vector) -> Tuple[float, float]:
    """
    Rigorous bracket on the Perron root from any strictly positive v:
        min_i (Av)_i / v_i  <=  r  <=  max_i (Av)_i / v_i.
    This makes the power iteration self-certifying.
    """
    Av = mat_vec(A, v)
    ratios = [Av[i] / v[i] for i in range(len(v))]
    return min(ratios), max(ratios)


def perron_sandwich(A: Matrix, v: Vector, r: float, n: int) -> Tuple[float, float, float]:
    """
    Return (c * P(n), r^n * sum(v), C * P(n)) where c = min v, C = max v.
    The Perron sandwich asserts the middle term lies between the outer two.
    """
    c, C = min(v), max(v)
    P = path_count(A, n)
    return c * P, (r ** n) * sum(v), C * P


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Automaton synthesis from a local (sliding-window) pruning rule
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def synthesize_automaton(b: int, window: int,
                         forbidden: Iterable[Sequence[int]]) -> Tuple[Matrix, List[Tuple[int, ...]]]:
    """
    Build the transition matrix of the pruning automaton for a rule of the form
    "the last `window` moves must never form a forbidden block", in a b-ary
    tree with alphabet {0, ..., b-1}.

    States are the legal words of length window-1; A[u][v] = 1 when v is
    obtained from u by appending a symbol and dropping the first, provided the
    resulting length-`window` block is not forbidden.  This is the standard
    sofic-subshift construction; the entropy of the resulting matrix is the
    topological entropy of the subshift.
    """
    forb = {tuple(f) for f in forbidden}

    def legal_word(w: Sequence[int]) -> bool:
        return all(tuple(w[i:i + window]) not in forb
                   for i in range(len(w) - window + 1))

    states: List[Tuple[int, ...]] = []
    def build(prefix: Tuple[int, ...]) -> None:
        if len(prefix) == window - 1:
            if legal_word(prefix):
                states.append(prefix)
            return
        for s in range(b):
            build(prefix + (s,))
    build(())

    index = {s: i for i, s in enumerate(states)}
    k = len(states)
    A: Matrix = [[0.0] * k for _ in range(k)]
    for u in states:
        for s in range(b):
            block = u + (s,)
            if tuple(block) in forb:
                continue
            nxt = block[1:]
            if nxt in index:
                A[index[u]][index[nxt]] += 1.0
    return A, states

# Demonstration 4: the Perron sandwich
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def demo_perron_sandwich() -> None:

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from typing import Callable, Iterable, List, Sequence, Tuple

Matrix = List[List[float]]
Vector = List[float]

SEP = "=" * 78
SUB = "-" * 78


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Basic linear algebra (pure Python, no dependencies)
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def mat_mul(A: Matrix, B: Matrix) -> Matrix:
    """Ordinary matrix product.  Cost O(k^3) for k x k inputs."""
    n, m, p = len(A), len(B), len(B[0])
    return [[sum(A[i][t] * B[t][j] for t in range(m)) for j in range(p)]
            for i in range(n)]


def mat_vec(A: Matrix, v: Vector) -> Vector:
    """Matrix-vector product A v.  Cost O(k^2)."""
    return [sum(A[i][j] * v[j] for j in range(len(v))) for i in range(len(A))]


def identity(k: int) -> Matrix:
    return [[1.0 if i == j else 0.0 for j in range(k)] for i in range(k)]


def mat_pow(A: Matrix, n: int) -> Matrix:
    """A^n by binary exponentiation.  Cost O(k^3 log n)."""
    result = identity(len(A))
    base = [row[:] for row in A]
    while n > 0:
        if n & 1:
            result = mat_mul(result, base)
        base = mat_mul(base, base)
        n >>= 1
    return result


def path_count(A: Matrix, n: int) -> float:
    """P(n) = sum of ALL entries of A^n: the number of accepted length-n paths."""
    return sum(sum(row) for row in mat_pow(A, n))


def path_counts_upto(A: Matrix, m: int) -> List[float]:
    """P(0), ..., P(m) in O(m k^2) by propagating the row-sum vector u = A^n 1."""
    k = len(A)
    u: Vector = [1.0] * k          # u = A^0 * 1
    out: List[float] = []
    for _ in range(m + 1):
        out.append(sum(u))
        u = mat_vec(A, u)
    return out


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The two headline constants
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

PHI: float = (1.0 + math.sqrt(5.0)) / 2.0          # golden ratio ~ 1.6180339887
FIB_MATRIX: Matrix = [[1.0, 1.0],
                      [1.0, 0.0]]                   # "no two expensive steps in a row"


def fibonacci(m: int) -> int:
    """F(1) = F(2) = 1, F(m+2) = F(m+1) + F(m); F(0) = 0."""
    a, b = 0, 1
    for _ in range(m):
        a, b = b, a + b
    return a


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Search profiles: entropy rate and proof-search dimension
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def finite_scale_rate(N: Callable[[int], float], n: int) -> float:
    """rate(n) = log N(n) / n, the average branching entropy out to depth n."""
    if n < 1:
        raise ValueError("finite-scale rates are defined for n >= 1")
    return math.log(N(n)) / n


def entropy_upper_bound(N: Callable[[int], float], depth: int) -> float:
    """
    CERTIFIED upper bound on the entropy rate: min over 1 <= n <= depth of
    log N(n) / n.  Because the Fekete limit is the INFIMUM of the finite-scale
    rates, this is not an estimate -- it is a proved bound on h, valid no
    matter how the profile behaves beyond `depth`.
    """
    return min(finite_scale_rate(N, n) for n in range(1, depth + 1))


def proof_search_dimension(entropy: float, b: float) -> float:
    """dim = h / log b, the ambient-normalized (fractal) dimension."""
    return entropy / math.log(b)


def check_submultiplicative(N: Callable[[int], float], bound: int) -> Tuple[bool, float]:
    """
    Verify N(m+n) <= N(m) N(n) for all 0 <= m, n <= bound and report the worst
    "defect ratio" N(m+n) / (N(m) N(n)) observed.  A ratio of 1 means the
    inequality is tight; smaller ratios measure how many (prefix, suffix)
    pairs fail to concatenate into a live path.
    """
    ok = True
    worst = 0.0
    for m in range(bound + 1):
        for n in range(bound + 1):
            lhs, rhs = N(m + n), N(m) * N(n)
            if lhs > rhs * (1 + 1e-12):
                ok = False
            worst = max(worst, lhs / rhs)
    return ok, worst


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Perron machinery
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def perron_root_power_iteration(
    A: Matrix, iters: int = 400, tol: float = 1e-15
) -> Tuple[float, Vector]:
    """
    Scaled power iteration x <- A x / ||A x||_1 from a positive start.
    Returns (r, v) with v normalized so that min(v) = 1.
    Cost O(k^2) per iteration; geometric convergence at rate |lambda_2| / r.
    """
    k = len(A)
    x: Vector = [1.0 / k] * k
    r = 0.0
    for _ in range(iters):
        y = mat_vec(A, x)
        norm = sum(abs(t) for t in y)
        if norm == 0.0:
            return 0.0, x
        new_x = [t / norm for t in y]
        if max(abs(new_x[i] - x[i]) for i in range(k)) < tol:
            x, r = new_x, norm
            break
        x, r = new_x, norm
    lo = min(x)
    v = [t / lo for t in x] if lo > 0 else x
    return r, v


def collatz_wielandt_bracket(A: Matrix, v: Vector) -> Tuple[float, float]:
    """
    Rigorous bracket on the Perron root from any strictly positive v:
        min_i (Av)_i / v_i  <=  r  <=  max_i (Av)_i / v_i.
    This makes the power iteration self-certifying.
    """
    Av = mat_vec(A, v)
    ratios = [Av[i] / v[i] for i in range(len(v))]
    return min(ratios), max(ratios)


def perron_sandwich(A: Matrix, v: Vector, r: float, n: int) -> Tuple[float, float, float]:
    """
    Return (c * P(n), r^n * sum(v), C * P(n)) where c = min v, C = max v.
    The Perron sandwich asserts the middle term lies between the outer two.
    """
    c, C = min(v), max(v)
    P = path_count(A, n)
    return c * P, (r ** n) * sum(v), C * P


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Automaton synthesis from a local (sliding-window) pruning rule
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def synthesize_automaton(b: int, window: int,
                         forbidden: Iterable[Sequence[int]]) -> Tuple[Matrix, List[Tuple[int, ...]]]:
    """
    Build the transition matrix of the pruning automaton for a rule of the form
    "the last `window` moves must never form a forbidden block", in a b-ary
    tree with alphabet {0, ..., b-1}.

    States are the legal words of length window-1; A[u][v] = 1 when v is
    obtained from u by appending a symbol and dropping the first, provided the
    resulting length-`window` block is not forbidden.  This is the standard
    sofic-subshift construction; the entropy of the resulting matrix is the
    topological entropy of the subshift.
    """
    forb = {tuple(f) for f in forbidden}

    def legal_word(w: Sequence[int]) -> bool:
        return all(tuple(w[i:i + window]) not in forb
                   for i in range(len(w) - window + 1))

    states: List[Tuple[int, ...]] = []
    def build(prefix: Tuple[int, ...]) -> None:
        if len(prefix) == window - 1:
            if legal_word(prefix):
                states.append(prefix)
            return
        for s in range(b):
            build(prefix + (s,))
    build(())

    index = {s: i for i, s in enumerate(states)}
    k = len(states)
    A: Matrix = [[0.0] * k for _ in range(k)]
    for u in states:
        for s in range(b):
            block = u + (s,)
            if tuple(block) in forb:
                continue
            nxt = block[1:]
            if nxt in index:
                A[index[u]][index[nxt]] += 1.0
    return A, states

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from typing import Callable, List, Tuple

Matrix = List[List[float]]


def mat_vec(A: Matrix, v: List[float]) -> List[float]:
    return [sum(A[i][j] * v[j] for j in range(len(v))) for i in range(len(A))]


def path_counts(A: Matrix, m: int) -> List[float]:
    u = [1.0] * len(A)
    out: List[float] = []
    for _ in range(m + 1):
        out.append(sum(u))
        u = mat_vec(A, u)
    return out


def perron(A: Matrix, iters: int = 6000) -> Tuple[float, List[float]]:
    k = len(A)
    x = [1.0 / k] * k
    r = 0.0
    for _ in range(iters):
        y = mat_vec(A, x)
        s = sum(y)
        if s == 0.0:
            return 0.0, x
        x = [t / s for t in y]
        r = s
    lo = min(x)
    return r, [t / lo for t in x]


def bracket_matrix(name: str, A: Matrix, depths: Tuple[int, ...]) -> None:

    print("  " + "-" * 66)

        upper = min(math.log(P[m]) / m for m in range(1, n + 1))
        lower = math.log(P[n]) / n - math.log(S / c) / n
        okay = "yes" if lower - 1e-12 <= h <= upper + 1e-12 else "NO"

              f"{upper-lower:>11.3e} {okay:>12}")

Computes a rigorous two-sided interval containing the entropy rate

the lower bound uses a positive eigenvector of the transition matrix.

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from typing import Callable, List, Optional, Sequence, Tuple

Matrix = List[List[float]]
Vector = List[float]


def entropy_upper_bound(N: Callable[[int], float], depth: int) -> float:
    """
    Rigorous UPPER bound on the entropy rate of any search profile.

    Valid because the Fekete limit equals the infimum of the finite-scale
    rates: h <= log N(n)/n for every n >= 1, with no error term.

    Complexity: `depth` evaluations of N.
    """
    if depth < 1:
        raise ValueError("depth must be at least 1")
    return min(math.log(N(n)) / n for n in range(1, depth + 1))


def matrix_path_counts(A: Matrix, depth: int) -> List[float]:
    """
    P(0), ..., P(depth) with P(n) = sum of all entries of A^n.

    Propagates the row-sum vector u = A^n * 1, so P(n) = <1, u>, giving
    O(depth * k^2) arithmetic operations instead of O(depth * k^3).
    """
    k = len(A)
    u: Vector = [1.0] * k
    out: List[float] = []
    for _ in range(depth + 1):
        out.append(sum(u))
        u = [sum(A[i][j] * u[j] for j in range(k)) for i in range(k)]
    return out


def entropy_bracket(
    A: Matrix, eigenvector: Vector, depth: int
) -> Tuple[float, float, float]:
    """
    Two-sided bracket (lower, upper, width) on the entropy of the automaton
    with nonnegative transition matrix `A`, given a strictly positive
    eigenvector `v`.

    Upper: h <= min_{1<=n<=depth} log P(n)/n            (Fekete infimum)
    Lower: the Perron sandwich gives P(n) <= (sum(v)/min(v)) r^n, hence
           log P(n)/n <= log r + log(sum(v)/min(v))/n, i.e.
           h = log r >= log P(depth)/depth - log(sum(v)/min(v))/depth.

    The bracket has width O(1/depth) with the constant log(max v / min v).

    Complexity: O(depth * k^2).
    """
    if min(eigenvector) <= 0.0:
        raise ValueError("the eigenvector must be strictly positive")
    P = matrix_path_counts(A, depth)
    if any(p <= 0.0 for p in P[: depth + 1]):
        raise ValueError("path counts must be positive")
    S, c = sum(eigenvector), min(eigenvector)
    upper = min(math.log(P[n]) / n for n in range(1, depth + 1))
    lower = math.log(P[depth]) / depth - math.log(S / c) / depth
    return lower, upper, upper - lower


def dimension_bracket(
    A: Matrix, eigenvector: Vector, depth: int, b: float
) -> Tuple[float, float]:
    """Normalize an entropy bracket by log b to bracket the proof-search dimension."""
    if b <= 1.0:
        raise ValueError("the ambient branching factor must exceed 1")
    lo, hi, _ = entropy_bracket(A, eigenvector, depth)
    logb = math.log(b)
    return lo / logb, hi / logb

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from typing import List, Optional, Tuple

Matrix = List[List[float]]
Vector = List[float]


def _mat_vec(A: Matrix, v: Vector) -> Vector:
    return [sum(A[i][j] * v[j] for j in range(len(v))) for i in range(len(A))]


def perron_root(
    A: Matrix, max_iters: int = 10_000, tol: float = 1e-15
) -> Tuple[float, Vector]:
    """
    Scaled power iteration:  x <- A x / ||A x||_1  from the uniform positive start.

    Returns (r, v) with v normalized so that min(v) = 1.  For a primitive matrix
    the iteration converges geometrically at rate |lambda_2| / r, where lambda_2
    is the second-largest eigenvalue in modulus.  Each iteration costs O(k^2).
    """
    k = len(A)
    if k == 0:
        raise ValueError("empty matrix")
    if any(A[i][j] < 0 for i in range(k) for j in range(k)):
        raise ValueError("the matrix must be entrywise nonnegative")
    x: Vector = [1.0 / k] * k
    r = 0.0
    for _ in range(max_iters):
        y = _mat_vec(A, x)
        norm = sum(abs(t) for t in y)
        if norm == 0.0:
            return 0.0, x
        nxt = [t / norm for t in y]
        delta = max(abs(nxt[i] - x[i]) for i in range(k))
        x, r = nxt, norm
        if delta < tol:
            break
    lo = min(x)
    v = [t / lo for t in x] if lo > 0.0 else x
    return r, v


def collatz_wielandt(A: Matrix, v: Vector) -> Tuple[float, float]:
    """
    From ANY strictly positive v, the Collatz-Wielandt inequalities give
        min_i (Av)_i / v_i  <=  r  <=  max_i (Av)_i / v_i.
    The bracket collapses to a point exactly when v is an eigenvector.
    """
    if min(v) <= 0.0:
        raise ValueError("v must be strictly positive")
    Av = _mat_vec(A, v)
    ratios = [Av[i] / v[i] for i in range(len(v))]
    return min(ratios), max(ratios)


def certified_perron(
    A: Matrix, max_iters: int = 10_000
) -> Tuple[float, Vector, Tuple[float, float]]:
    """Perron root, eigenvector, and a certified enclosing interval for the root."""
    r, v = perron_root(A, max_iters)
    return r, v, collatz_wielandt(A, v)


def proof_search_dimension(A: Matrix, b: float) -> Tuple[float, Tuple[float, float]]:
    """
    Proof-search dimension log r / log b of a finite-state pruned search inside a
    b-ary ambient tree, with a certified enclosure inherited from Collatz-Wielandt.
    """
    if b <= 1.0:
        raise ValueError("the ambient branching factor must exceed 1")
    r, _, (lo, hi) = certified_perron(A)
    logb = math.log(b)
    if r <= 0.0:
        return 0.0, (0.0, 0.0)
    return math.log(r) / logb, (math.log(lo) / logb, math.log(hi) / logb)

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from typing import Dict, Iterable, List, Sequence, Set, Tuple

Matrix = List[List[float]]
State = Tuple[int, ...]


def _legal(word: Sequence[int], w: int, forbidden: Set[State]) -> bool:
    """True when no length-w window of `word` is forbidden."""
    return all(tuple(word[i:i + w]) not in forbidden
               for i in range(len(word) - w + 1))


def synthesize_automaton(
    b: int, w: int, forbidden: Iterable[Sequence[int]]
) -> Tuple[Matrix, List[State]]:
    """
    Build the transition matrix and the state list.

    The matrix has at most b^(w-1) rows and at most b nonzero entries per row,
    so construction costs O(b^w) time and O(b^(2w-2)) space for the dense matrix
    (O(b^w) if stored sparsely).
    """
    if b < 1 or w < 1:
        raise ValueError("b and w must be positive")
    forb: Set[State] = {tuple(f) for f in forbidden}

    states: List[State] = []

    def extend(prefix: State) -> None:
        if len(prefix) == w - 1:
            if _legal(prefix, w, forb):
                states.append(prefix)
            return
        for s in range(b):
            extend(prefix + (s,))

    extend(())
    index: Dict[State, int] = {s: i for i, s in enumerate(states)}
    k = len(states)
    A: Matrix = [[0.0] * k for _ in range(k)]
    for u in states:
        for s in range(b):
            block = u + (s,)
            if tuple(block) in forb:
                continue
            nxt = block[1:]
            j = index.get(nxt)
            if j is not None:
                A[index[u]][j] += 1.0
    return A, states


def prune_unreachable(A: Matrix) -> Matrix:
    """
    Iteratively delete states with no outgoing transition (dead ends).  Repeating
    to a fixed point leaves the subgraph on which infinite paths actually live,
    which is the part that determines the Perron root.  Cost O(k^3) worst case.
    """
    keep = list(range(len(A)))
    changed = True
    while changed:
        changed = False
        alive = [i for i in keep if any(A[i][j] > 0 for j in keep)]
        if len(alive) != len(keep):
            keep, changed = alive, True
    return [[A[i][j] for j in keep] for i in keep]


def dimension_of_rule(
    b: int, w: int, forbidden: Iterable[Sequence[int]], iters: int = 6000
) -> float:
    """

    scaled power iteration, and return the proof-search dimension log r / log b.

    A, states = synthesize_automaton(b, w, forbidden)
    A = prune_unreachable(A)
    k = len(A)
    if k == 0:
        return 0.0
    x: List[float] = [1.0 / k] * k
    r = 0.0
    for _ in range(iters):
        y = [sum(A[i][j] * x[j] for j in range(k)) for i in range(k)]

        if s == 0.0:
            return 0.0
        x = [t / s for t in y]
        r = s
    return math.log(r) / math.log(b) if r > 0 else 0.0

def survives(word: Tuple[int, ...]) -> bool:

from __future__ import annotations

import itertools
import math
from typing import List, Sequence, Set, Tuple

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

Matrix = List[List[float]]


def mat_vec(A: Matrix, v: List[float]) -> List[float]:
    return [sum(A[i][j] * v[j] for j in range(len(v))) for i in range(len(A))]


def perron_root(A: Matrix, iters: int = 4000) -> float:
    k = len(A)
    if k == 0:
        return 0.0
    x = [1.0 / k] * k
    r = 0.0
    for _ in range(iters):
        y = mat_vec(A, x)
        s = sum(y)
        if s == 0.0:
            return 0.0
        x = [t / s for t in y]
        r = s
    return r


def synthesize_w2(b: int, forbidden: Set[Tuple[int, int]]) -> Matrix:
    """Window length 2: states are the b symbols; A[u][v] = 1 unless (u,v) forbidden."""
    return [[0.0 if (u, v) in forbidden else 1.0 for v in range(b)] for u in range(b)]


def spectrum(b: int) -> List[Tuple[int, float, Sequence[Tuple[int, int]]]]:
    pairs = list(itertools.product(range(b), repeat=2))
    out: List[Tuple[int, float, Sequence[Tuple[int, int]]]] = []
    for k in range(len(pairs) + 1):
        for forb in itertools.combinations(pairs, k):
            A = synthesize_w2(b, set(forb))
            r = perron_root(A)
            if r <= 0:
                continue
            out.append((k, math.log(r) / math.log(b), forb))
    return out

    phi = (1 + math.sqrt(5)) / 2

### A guided tour: from pruning heuristics to the golden ratio, by way of Fekete's lemma and the Perron root

---

## 0. Where we are going

Every automated reasoning system lives inside a tree. The root is a goal; each node offers finitely many inference steps; each step spawns a child. If every node offers $b$ moves, then depth $n$ holds $b^n$ nodes — an astronomically large space almost immediately.

What rescues the situation is **pruning**: most branches die early and take their entire subtrees with them. The surviving structure is a sparse, irregular subtree, and this page is about the single number that measures how sparse it is.

By the end you will be able to say, precisely and quantitatively, what it means for a pruning heuristic to "help", and you will be able to compute the answer for any pruning rule with bounded memory. Along the way the golden ratio will appear, unbidden, out of the simplest nontrivial rule you can write down.

> **The punchline, stated up front.** Let $N(n)$ count the search prefixes of length $n$ that are still alive. Then the limit
> $$h \;=\; \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log N(n)}{n}$$
> always exists (under hypotheses so weak that essentially every real search satisfies them), it equals the *infimum* of the quantities $\log N(n)/n$, and the normalized value $\dim = h/\log b$ lies in $[0,1]$. When the pruning is implementable with finite memory, $\dim = \log r/\log b$ where $r$ is the Perron eigenvalue of the pruning automaton's transition matrix.

---

## 1. Play first, theorize later

Before any definitions, get your hands on the object. Below is a laboratory: choose an ambient branching factor, forbid some blocks of moves, and watch the dimension of the resulting search space appear.

Try these in order:

1. **Forbid nothing.** Dimension $1$. No pruning, no saving.
2. **Binary, forbid the block `11`.** Dimension $0.694242\ldots$ — and if you look at the Perron root, it is $1.618033\ldots$, the golden ratio. (This is the "golden preset" button.)

4. **Ternary, forbid `22`.** Dimension $0.914838\ldots$ — one forbidden block out of nine barely dents the exponent.

## 2. Two axioms, and nothing else

Let $T$ be the set of live search prefixes — a prefix-closed subtree of the full $b$-ary tree — and let $N(n)$ be the number of elements of $T$ of length $n$.

**Axiom 1 (nondegeneracy).** $N(n) \ge 1$ for every $n$: there is always at least one live path.

**Axiom 2 (submultiplicativity).** $N(m+n) \le N(m)\,N(n)$.

<details>
<summary><b>Why submultiplicativity is essentially free</b> (click to expand)</summary>

A surviving path of length $m+n$ is determined by two pieces of data: its length-$m$ prefix, and the length-$n$ continuation that follows. There are at most $N(m)$ choices for the first piece. For the second, note that in any search language whose pruning rule depends only on *bounded local data* — which is to say, any realistic one — the set of legal continuations from a live state is again a search language of the same kind, so there are at most $N(n)$ of them.

Multiplying gives $N(m+n) \le N(m)N(n)$. The inequality is typically **strict**, sometimes very much so, because most (prefix, suffix) pairs simply do not concatenate into a live word. That slack is not a defect: it is what makes the theory interesting, since a submultiplicative sequence can be far from a geometric one.

It is worth pausing on how little is being assumed. No self-similarity. No monotonicity. No recursion. No regularity of any kind. The counts may fluctuate wildly from level to level. Everything below follows from these two lines.
</details>

A function $N : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying both axioms is called a **search profile**, and the quantity
$$\mathrm{rate}(n) \;=\; \frac{\log N(n)}{n} \qquad (n \ge 1)$$
is its **finite-scale rate**: the average branching entropy measured out to depth $n$.

---

## 3. Fekete's descent

Here is the first theorem.

> **Search Entropy Theorem.** For every search profile,
> $$\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log N(n)}{n} \;=\; \inf_{n\ge 1}\frac{\log N(n)}{n} \;=:\; h \;\ge\; 0.$$

Two separate assertions live in that display, and the second is the one that matters practically.

<details>
<summary><b>Proof sketch: Fekete's subadditive lemma</b></summary>

Set $a_n = \log N(n)$. Taking logarithms of Axiom 2 turns submultiplicativity into **subadditivity**:
$$a_{m+n} \;\le\; a_m + a_n.$$
Axiom 1 gives $a_n \ge 0$, so the ratios $a_n/n$ are bounded below by $0$; let $L = \inf_{n\ge1} a_n/n$, a finite number.

Fix $\varepsilon > 0$ and choose $m$ with $a_m/m < L + \varepsilon$. Write an arbitrary $n$ as $n = qm + s$ with $0 \le s < m$. Iterating subadditivity $q$ times,
$$a_n \;\le\; q\,a_m + a_s,\qquad\text{so}\qquad \frac{a_n}{n} \;\le\; \frac{qm}{n}\cdot\frac{a_m}{m} + \frac{a_s}{n}.$$
As $n \to \infty$ with $m$ fixed, $qm/n \to 1$ and $a_s/n \to 0$ (only $m$ different values of $a_s$ ever occur). Hence $\limsup_n a_n/n \le a_m/m < L+\varepsilon$. Since $\varepsilon$ was arbitrary, $\limsup_n a_n/n \le L$. The matching $\liminf_n a_n/n \ge L$ is immediate from the definition of the infimum. $\blacksquare$

The mechanism is worth internalizing: subadditivity lets you *tile* a long interval with copies of a good short one, and the leftover is bounded, so it disappears after division by $n$.
</details>

The second assertion — that the limit **is** the infimum — has a consequence that turns a piece of asymptotic analysis into a practical tool:

$$\boxed{\;h \;\le\; \frac{\log N(n)}{n}\quad \text{for every } n \ge 1.\;}$$

**Any single finite computation is a proved upper bound on the asymptotic entropy.** Not an estimate, not an extrapolation: a theorem. Run your search to depth $17$, count $N(17) = 4096$ survivors, and you have established $h \le \log 4096 / 17 \approx 0.4895$ for all time. This is the rare situation where a heuristic measurement is simultaneously a rigorous bound.

The picture below shows the descent for four different pruning rules. Every gold curve sits strictly above its own dashed limit, and the excess decays like $O(1/n)$.

## 4. From a rate to a dimension

The entropy $h$ has units — nats per level. Normalizing against the ambient tree gives a dimensionless number.

> **Definition.** The **proof-search dimension** of a search profile relative to an ambient branching factor $b > 1$ is
> $$\dim \;=\; \frac{h}{\log b}.$$
>
> **Dimension bounds.** $\dim \ge 0$ always, and $\dim \le 1$ whenever $N(n) \le b^n$.

<details>
<summary><b>Why the upper bound is a one-liner</b></summary>

Apply the hypothesis at $n = 1$: $N(1) \le b$, so $\mathrm{rate}(1) = \log N(1) \le \log b$. Since $h$ is the *infimum* of the finite-scale rates, $h \le \mathrm{rate}(1) \le \log b$. Divide by $\log b > 0$. $\blacksquare$

Notice that the argument used only the bound at scale $1$. That is the infimum characterization doing all the work: it lets a single-scale fact control the asymptotics.
</details>

This is not merely *like* a fractal dimension — it is the same formula. The middle-thirds Cantor set keeps $2$ of every $3$ subintervals and has similarity dimension $\log 2/\log 3 \approx 0.6309$; a search keeping $2$ of every $3$ branches has proof-search dimension $\log 2/\log 3$. The set of infinite live paths, sitting inside the boundary $\{1,\dots,b\}^{\mathbb{N}}$ with the ultrametric $d(x,y) = b^{-|x\wedge y|}$, is a genuinely Cantor-like compact set: the ball of radius $b^{-n}$ around a point is exactly the depth-$n$ cylinder, and $N(n)$ is exactly the number of such balls needed to cover the boundary.

Here is that picture for the Fibonacci rule — the pruned tree, its Cantor-like boundary, and the exponential decay of the surviving fraction.

{{visualization:1}}

*Learn more:* [Fekete's subadditive lemma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subadditivity), [Hausdorff dimension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hausdorff_dimension), [the Cantor set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantor_set).

## 5. Making it computable: matrices enter

So far we have an existence theorem. To get *numbers*, restrict to pruning rules with bounded memory.

Suppose the legality of a move depends only on which of $k$ states the search is in, and taking a move updates the state. That is a finite automaton, with **transition matrix**
$$A_{ij} \;=\; \#\{\text{legal moves carrying state } i \text{ to state } j\} \;\ge\; 0.$$
Powers of $A$ count paths: $(A^n)_{ij}$ is the number of accepted length-$n$ paths from $i$ to $j$, so the total is
$$P(n) \;=\; \sum_{i,j}(A^n)_{ij}.$$

> **Path counts are submultiplicative.** For any nonnegative square matrix $A$ and any $m,n \ge 0$: $P(m+n) \le P(m)P(n)$.

<details>
<summary><b>Proof: a two-line rearrangement</b></summary>

For each intermediate state $\ell$ let $f(\ell) = \sum_i (A^m)_{i\ell}$ (length-$m$ paths *ending* at $\ell$) and $g(\ell) = \sum_j (A^n)_{\ell j}$ (length-$n$ paths *starting* at $\ell$). Both are nonnegative, and $P(m) = \sum_\ell f(\ell)$, $P(n) = \sum_\ell g(\ell)$.

Expanding $A^{m+n} = A^m A^n$ and reordering the finite triple sum,
$$P(m+n) \;=\; \sum_\ell f(\ell)\,g(\ell),\qquad\text{whereas}\qquad P(m)P(n) \;=\; \sum_\ell f(\ell)\Big(\sum_{\ell'} g(\ell')\Big).$$
Since every $g(\ell') \ge 0$, we have $g(\ell) \le \sum_{\ell'}g(\ell')$ term by term; multiply by $f(\ell) \ge 0$ and sum. $\blacksquare$

In words: concatenation requires the endpoint of the first path to match the start of the second, but the product $P(m)P(n)$ pays for *all* pairings. The defect is exactly the mismatched pairs.
</details>

So every finite-state pruned search is a search profile, and the Search Entropy Theorem applies. Now we can do better than "the limit exists".

## 6. The Perron sandwich

Enter the spectral theory of nonnegative matrices — Perron (1907), Frobenius (1912).

Suppose $A$ has a **strictly positive eigenvector**: a vector $v$ with $0 < c \le v_i \le C$ and $Av = rv$ for some $r > 0$. For a strongly connected automaton, Perron–Frobenius theory guarantees one exists, with $r$ the largest eigenvalue — the **Perron root**.

> **Perron sandwich.** For every $n \ge 0$:
> $$c\,P(n) \;\le\; r^n \sum_i v_i \;\le\; C\,P(n).$$

<details>
<summary><b>Proof: no spectral decomposition required</b></summary>

Since $Av = rv$, induction gives $A^n v = r^n v$, i.e. for each row $i$,
$$\sum_j (A^n)_{ij}\,v_j \;=\; r^n v_i.$$
All entries $(A^n)_{ij}$ are nonnegative (also by induction). Replace $v_j$ on the left by its lower bound $c$: the sum can only decrease, giving $c\sum_j (A^n)_{ij} \le r^n v_i$. Sum over $i$ for the left inequality. Replace $v_j$ by its upper bound $C$ instead, and the same argument in reverse gives the right one. $\blacksquare$

No Jordan form, no complex analysis, no assumption that $r$ is the *largest* eigenvalue. One eigenvector with coordinates bounded away from $0$ and $\infty$ is the entire analytic input.
</details>

Equivalently, with $S = \sum_i v_i$:
$$\frac{S}{C}\,r^n \;\le\; P(n) \;\le\; \frac{S}{c}\,r^n.$$
The path counts are exponential with base *exactly* $r$, up to a bounded fluctuation whose width is the "spread" $C/c$ of the eigenvector.

Play with this below. Enter any nonnegative $2\times2$ matrix and watch the ratio $P(n)/r^n$ stay locked inside the blue band forever. Then try the **reducible** preset $\begin{pmatrix}3&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ and observe what happens when the positive-eigenvector hypothesis fails.

## 7. The Bridge Theorem

Take logarithms of the sandwich and divide by $n$. The constants $S/C$ and $S/c$ contribute $O(1/n)$ and vanish.

> **Bridge Theorem.** For a nonnegative matrix with a strictly positive eigenvector for an eigenvalue $r > 0$,
> $$\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log P(n)}{n} \;=\; \log r,$$
> and hence, relative to an ambient $b$-ary tree,
> $$\dim \;=\; \frac{\log r}{\log b}.$$

Three worlds meet here. **Combinatorics** supplies the object — accepted paths in a pruned tree. **Analysis** guarantees the measurement converges — Fekete. **Linear algebra** supplies the answer — the Perron root.

And because the Bridge Theorem identifies $h$ with $\log r$, while Fekete identifies $h$ with an *infimum*, we can run the whole thing backwards:

> **Perron Domination Inequality.** Under the same hypotheses, for **every** $n \ge 0$,
> $$r^n \;\le\; \sum_{i,j}(A^n)_{ij}.$$

<details>
<summary><b>Why this is surprising</b></summary>

There are no limits in that statement. No asymptotics, no error term, no epsilon. It is a finite inequality about matrix powers, valid at every single $n$. Yet the proof goes:

$$\log r \;=\; h \;\le\; \frac{\log P(n)}{n} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad n\log r \le \log P(n) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad r^n \le P(n).$$

An asymptotic quantity — the entropy — was used to derive a uniform finite bound, and the only reason this works is that Fekete's limit is an *infimum*, hence simultaneously a lower bound on every finite-scale rate. Information flowed from $n = \infty$ back to every finite $n$.
</details>

---

## 8. The golden ratio, hiding in a search tree

Now cash it out. Take a **binary** search tree and impose one bit of memory:

> **Never use two "expensive" inference steps in a row.**

(Never two consecutive case splits; never invoke the heavy decision procedure twice running.) Two states suffice — "last step was cheap" and "last step was expensive" — with transition matrix
$$A = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 1\\ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix}.$$

Three facts fall out, each a short computation:

- **The path counts are Fibonacci numbers.** From $A^2 = A + I$ one gets $P(n+2) = P(n+1) + P(n)$, and with $P(0)=2$, $P(1)=3$ this gives $P(n) = F_{n+3}$: the counts are $2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, 34, 55, \dots$
- **The Perron root is the golden ratio.** $(\varphi, 1)$ is a strictly positive eigenvector with eigenvalue $\varphi = (1+\sqrt5)/2$, because $\varphi^2 = \varphi + 1$.
- **The dimension is $\log\varphi/\log 2 \approx 0.694242$.** By the Bridge Theorem.

And the domination inequality specializes to a classical fact, obtained here entirely by detour:
$$\varphi^{\,n} \;\le\; F_{n+3}\qquad\text{for every } n \ge 0.$$

Verify all three, with exact integer arithmetic and a rational under-approximation of $\varphi$ so that nothing rests on floating point:

**What a dimension of $0.694$ actually buys you.** At depth $100$ the unpruned binary tree has $2^{100} \approx 1.27\times 10^{30}$ nodes; the pruned tree has $F_{103} \approx 1.5\times10^{21}$ — more than eight orders of magnitude fewer, with the gap growing like $2^{0.3058\,n}$. Pruning does not turn an exponential problem polynomial. It lowers the **base** of the exponential, and the dimension records exactly by how much.

*Learn more:* [Perron–Frobenius theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perron%E2%80%93Frobenius_theorem), [the golden ratio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_ratio), [subshifts of finite type](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subshift_of_finite_type).

## 9. Which dimensions are achievable?

Sweep over all rules that forbid some set of length-$2$ blocks and plot the resulting dimensions. The picture is not a smooth spread: the achievable values cluster, because what matters is the Perron root of the surviving transition structure, not the raw count of surviving moves. Forbidding four of nine ternary blocks can leave you anywhere from dimension $0$ to $0.63$.

{{visualization:2}}

This raises a genuine open question, discussed in §12: the achievable numbers are exactly the normalized logarithms $\log r/\log b$ of Perron roots of nonnegative integer matrices — a restrictive and well-studied class of algebraic numbers. Classifying them would classify the possible "sizes" of finite-state-prunable search spaces.

## 10. Turning the theory into a measurement

Two algorithms do all the practical work.

The first produces a **certified two-sided bracket** on the entropy from finitely many prefix counts. The upper half needs nothing but submultiplicativity; the lower half uses the Perron sandwich, and the bracket narrows at rate $O(1/n)$ with constant $\log(C/c)$.

{{algorithm:0}}

The second extracts the Perron root itself and, crucially, **certifies its own answer**: given the computed eigenvector $v$, the Collatz–Wielandt inequalities
$$\min_i \frac{(Av)_i}{v_i} \;\le\; r \;\le\; \max_i \frac{(Av)_i}{v_i}$$
bracket the true root rigorously, and the bracket collapses to a point exactly when $v$ is an eigenvector.

{{algorithm:1}}

## 11. What the number does *not* know

Two honest caveats, both instructive.

<details>
<summary><b>Dimension measures abundance, not difficulty</b></summary>

The entropy depends only on the counting function, hence only on the *geometry* of the search space. It is completely invariant under any rearrangement of the tree that preserves level counts.

So two search problems can have identical prefix counts at every depth — hence identical dimension — while a depth-first traversal finds the proof immediately in one and only after an astronomical detour in the other.

$$\text{search cost} \;=\; \text{geometry} \times \text{policy},$$

and the dimension isolates the first factor. Far from a weakness, this is the point: it quantifies exactly the part of the difficulty that *no* clever traversal order can remove. Demonstration 10 in the comprehensive suite below makes the separation concrete.
</details>

<details>
<summary><b>Sparse damage does not matter</b></summary>

Change the branching structure at a set of depths of asymptotic density zero — say one level in a million behaves anomalously — and the logarithmic volumes shift by a sublinear amount. The entropy is unchanged.

The dimension is a robust, asymptotic quantity, insensitive to any bounded amount of local weirdness. That is precisely what one wants from a measure of intrinsic size, and it is why the theory survives contact with real search systems, which are full of special cases.
</details>
